The next day he had come and had sat there for an hour, talking quietly with her. He strove to be as entertaining as possible, told her about the Swedish actors and about a concert that some Polish artists had given. He suggested that she hear the French singers at Tivoli, but she had no desire to. He was determined to speak about something that amused her, and it really did seem that he was having some success. She listened to him kindly, asked about one thing and another, and thanked him at parting for the visit. He left her with a feeling that his presence had at least not been unpleasant to her, and on the stairs he considered how soon he might come again.

He waited a fortnight. She was at home and received him with a couple of polite words, but it was impossible for him to read from her expression whether the sight of him was welcome or unwelcome to her. He had hoped to come a little closer to her this time, but in that he was disappointed. His attempts to awaken her interest in what was going on and in what people were occupied with at the time were met with such measured answers that he became afraid of boring her. Then he fell silent so that she might begin talking about something; but then she merely made a few remarks about the weather, which were followed by a painful pause. He turned the conversation to the theater, but when she replied that she never went there and therefore had no interest in it,

20*

his courage sank. What could he possibly think of when faced with this hidden and closed-off woman? He left her with a melancholy feeling that he stood farther from her than ever before.—

When he was gone, Constance sat thinking how nice and agreeable he was. He gave an entirely different impression now than he had then; that was certain. Her aversion had disappeared, and deep down she felt a sort of fondness for him.

But even so, what did she want with his visits? She would rather do without them. It was too bothersome to sit there stiffly and have to answer and think of something to ask. And in general she did not like being disturbed when she sat occupied with her own thoughts. Why could they not leave her in peace?

She went out of the room and opened the kitchen door.

“Are you there, Johanne?” she asked.

Johanne demonstrated her presence by appearing in the doorway of the maid’s room.

“You recognize the gentleman you let in today, don’t you?”

“Doctor Lorck? Yes, goodness, of course.”

“If he comes again, I am not at home. Now do not forget that.”

“No, I shall be sure to remember,” said Johanne.

A month had passed, and in the course of it Lorck had tried in vain to see Constance three times. Then one day a letter came for her with the following contents:

Mrs. Constance Ring!

I have called on you several times without finding you at home; so I must try writing. But I am so afraid of offending or frightening you that I do not know how to couch my words. What I wish to tell you is that I have now pondered deeply over myself and you for a long time, and that I know in the depths of my soul that I love you with a love that would be worthy of you. With you lies happiness in life for me. If you will have nothing to do with me, I shall not find it on this earth.

If you could come to trust me, do you not think it might be possible for me, in time, to win your love?

Your most devoted,
Nils Lorck.

She was immensely surprised by his letter, but when she thought it over, it seemed to her so foolish that she had not understood before what he meant.

She replied at once:

Dear Dr. Lorck!

You must not be angry with me, but I do not think it is worthwhile for you to waste your time trying to win my love. It would be unworthy if, in order to obtain a little variety in my monotonous life, I began experimenting with myself and made use of you for that purpose. For it would be nothing else if I invited you to make a trial. I esteem you too highly for that, and I have not the slightest desire for it either. Do not think that I bear you any ill will; the opposite is the case. Of that you must be entirely convinced.

Yours,
Constance Ring.

About half a year had passed. Early in the winter, old District Judge Blom had died, and his wife had then gone to stay with her youngest daughter, who was married to a pastor at Nordfjordeidet. The childhood home had thus been broken up; the two brothers were each in his own place, and the other sister was living with her future parents-in-law in Molde.

Constance had been painfully affected by the news of her father’s death. It was as though the image of her happy childhood and early youth had perished at the same time. Now her dear father lay in the grave, and the other inhabitants of the beloved home were scattered to the four winds. There was no longer any fixed point to which she could attach her dreams and longings, no sheltered spot to which she could turn in thought in her most dejected moments. Everything had been swept away; she was so poor and bereft, her life so desolate and meaningless, and she often thought it would be best to die.—

They talked about Mejer and were both elated by their meeting with him. Constance thought he had changed so much, not for the better, she believed. He was so blasé and spoke so mockingly about himself and everything. Lorck replied that this was what happened to artists who were condemned to live in Norway. “It is a pity about him, though,” he added, “for he is a fine and splendid fellow. I have always liked him so much.”

“Yes, so have I,” said Constance. “I wish he would marry a rich lady.”

“Shall we put our heads together and see if we can find him one?” Lorck asked with a smile.

Constance laughed.

“When we get home, we must be really nice to him, Constance. I think he likes being with us.”

“Yes, really nice,” Constance replied.

“By the way, he was surely madly smitten with you for a time, you know. Did you not notice anything?”

“Not a trace,” was the answer.

“Did he never let anything of the sort be known?”

“Never!” Constance replied.

“No, he is a refined and well-bred person,” Lorck thought, and offered a silent sigh to the memory of his own conduct.

“It was probably only a quite passing fit that he had, anyway,” he said aloud.

“Did he say anything to you about it, then?” Constance asked with a half-roguish, half-bashful smile.

“No indeed, not the slightest blessed thing,” Lorck assured her. “It may well be that it was merely a fancy of mine. I went around thinking that everyone was bound to fall in love with you, you see.”

They were both silent for a few minutes.

“What are you thinking about, my Conny?” Lorck then said, searching for her hand.

“Nothing, really,” she said kindly.

“Nonsense, tell me now,” he begged, drawing her closer to him.

“Well, that is easier said than done. Sometimes one’s thoughts run so wild, or they come in little fragments and are so disconnected, or it is sheer foolishness that one sits there being whirled around by; it is simply impossible to find words for it.”

He had put his arm around her waist and, with his other hand, bent her head toward him so that it came to rest against his neck. They held each other in an embrace and sat for a while without speaking.

“But now I know what I am thinking about,” said Constance, pressing her lips against his beard.

“About what, Conny?”

“About what we have spoken of so often: about how happy you have made me, about all our treasures, about everything we have experienced together, about the love you have loved into being in me, and above all about what you know—the thing that lies ahead.”

“My beloved, my sweet,” Lorck said, pressing her closer to him. “How happy you make me; how blissful your words are, and how sweet your caresses. And you, who were so afraid to take me—” he added a little later in a more tender voice.

“Not you any more than others. I felt reluctance or distaste, in general, altogether.”

“You naughty thing, who wanted nothing to do with me. Can you remember how I had to strive? And if the letter had not—ugh, I dare not think of it.”

“It was a dreadful time,” said Constance. “What a creature I had become. That you truly had the courage to take me on was well done of you”—she clung to him.

“I loved you, Conny.”

“And at the beginning, when we were married, can you remember how foolish I was—quite wretched with shyness?”

“Really, I have been quite persevering, Conny; you must admit that, for you did everything to discourage me. But, as I said, I loved you. I had never loved before I began to love you.”

“Is that really true, Nils? Tell me, is it true?”

“Yes, my friend, I know that now. If it had not been for you, I would never have learned to know love. And now that we are expecting our treasure, I am overjoyed, Conny.”

“But you have been in love with others, surely—yes, and had relations with others?”

“That was foolishness and nonsense, Conny. It is you who first made life come alive for me.”

“And it is the same for you, Conny,” he continued a little later. “Your life begins only with me, does it not?”

She did not answer.

“You need rest, you must sleep,” she said,
and, to satisfy him and lull him to
sleep, she began to stroke him through
his curly hair, gently, softly, more and more
slowly. That night Lorck slept peacefully and
uninterruptedly for the first time since he became
bedridden. It was clear that the illness
had taken a favorable turn.

But no sleep came to Constance.
She so dearly wished to find oblivion from the

torment she was suffering, and lay so still, so still, with
closed eyes, now and then changed position,
tried lying on her back with her knees
drawn up in an arch, turned over and lay
with her face buried in the pillow, but no, it
would not succeed. At last she got up to
try walking up and down in the
other room until she grew tired or began
to feel cold; then sleep would surely come.
She slipped her bare feet into a pair of slippers, threw
on a skirt and a dressing jacket, and stole
quietly out of the bedroom.

A pale, strangely dead and silent morning
light filled the room. Through the open balcony
doors came a thousand-voiced chorus of twittering
birds. She stepped out onto the balcony; it
was wet with dew, and the sky was gray-blue and
hazy. Not a breath of air could be felt;
trees and plants seemed to stand sleeping, and
the water lay stretching out in the deepest
repose. In the eastern sky there were narrow, yellowish
streaks; the sun would soon be there. This
silence was oppressive. Constance shuddered and
huddled up. Her thoughts revolved around
this one thing: this woman whom he had
loved and lived with, and who had given
him a child.

Could he have loved Kristine as he
now loved her? Could he have—could
he have? She writhed beneath the thoughts.

Suddenly she remembered the package; it had to
be letters. Hansen had spoken of some words of
farewell.

“O most merciful God and Creator,” she
said in an audible whisper, “there are letters,
letters!”

She raised her eyebrows and opened
her eyes wide as if in alarm; she pursed her lips
to a point and whistled very softly. An anguish-mingled
rapture seized her;
she wanted to throw herself upon the letters and read like
one possessed. She did not feel a second’s hesitation
or a shadow of scruple; on the contrary,
she knew within herself that nothing in the world
would be able to hinder or stop her. An
expression of cruelty lay about her mouth,
the blood hammered in her temples, and her hands
trembled as she cut the wrapping apart.

On top lay a letter written in a clumsy
hand and with extremely confused spelling.

“Dear Nils”—it said—“I beg
your pardon most sincerely for daring to write
to you after all this time, but it is to inform
you that God has taken our beloved son home to Him,
and although I know well that it was the best
thing that could befall my poor, blessed Anton,
since he was fatherless, though his father
was alive, which is even worse, I nevertheless feel
a bitter sorrow over his passing.

For he was my all and my joy, and he
was the very image of his father, and I know
that it is not pleasing to you now, since you are
married and no longer love me, but it was
a heartfelt joy to me to see this likeness,
for I could not stop loving you when
you left me and set your heart upon
another. Alas for me, it was my torment,
but also my joy, and I love you to this
day just as deeply as at the time when you
called me your little kitten and said that my
love was your comfort and happiness. And when
I think of all the lovely evenings and
nights I spent with you, my tears flow,
and they will do so always, for I shall not
forget you in this life. But enough of this;
my sweet, dear boy died a week ago today,
and was buried on the fifth day.
His coffin was so pretty, and it was quite
full of flowers, and he was exactly
one year and eight months old to the day, for he was born
in January, after you had left in October, if you
remember. It was typhus he had, and he
suffered dreadful pains. Shortly before he died,
he opened his eyes and looked at me as though
he wished to lament to me, and it pierced my heart
that I had brought him into the world in shame;
I bent over him and spoke to him,
though I was choked with weeping, and then he smiled
so sweetly, and then he drew breath heavily

and died. I thought my heart had broken
at that very moment, but what a human being can
endure in suffering is unbelievable. And now I will
say my last farewell to you; I am going to Drammen,
where, as you remember, I have family; I think
I shall be able to find work there. I shall never see
you again in this world, but think of you,
that I shall often do, and of him
for whom I have suffered and wept so much. I
sincerely wish that you may always remain
happy, and that she who is your wife may
love you as deeply as I did; then you
will not lack love. And so, in closing,
thank you for everything. To you I owe it that I have tasted
happiness in life; though it was brief and ended
in bitter sorrow, I would not have been without
it, no, never. And I bless
you because you have provided so well for our child.
Farewell, then, and may you fare as well as is wished
for you by your old faithful
Kristine.”

When Constance had read the letter, she laid her
face in her hands and sobbed. This
poor woman with her child! Why had she
been cast off? By what right did men behave
in this way! They enjoyed these women’s youth,
their health, their love, as though
they had been created for this one purpose; they enjoyed them until
they were sated. If they saw something more

desirable, they flung them aside and
abandoned them to the fate that the men’s
brutal selfishness had prepared for them. She felt
a profound compassion for this patient
sufferer, who was so full of goodness and resignation,
and at the same time a rebellious bitterness against
the brutality of society that had made it so
convenient and so free of danger for men to
indulge their sexual lusts.

She no longer felt any jealousy;
the nature of her pain was different; a
violent aversion to her husband stirred within
her—she could not bear to think of him.

The remaining letters were from Lorck to Kristine;
they were numbered, and she read them in order.
She saw that it was a relationship that had
lasted for several years, but at the same time he had had
love affairs on the side, as was evident
from answers he had given to Kristine’s reproaches
and outbursts of jealousy.
One of these rivals had been a married

affair. If you had not happened
to learn of it, it could not have done
you any harm. Besides, I am tired of this constant
being on guard against the husband,

It was typhus he had, and he suffered dreadful pains. I thought my heart had burst then and there, but what a human being can endure in the way of suffering is incredible. And now I shall bid you my final farewell; I am going to Drammen, where, as you remember, I have family; I think I shall be able to find work there. I shall never see you again in this world, but I shall often think of you, and of him for whom I have suffered and wept so much. I sincerely wish that you may always be happy, and that she who is your wife may love you just as dearly as I did; then you will not lack love. And finally, thank you for everything. It is to you that I owe having tasted happiness in life; though it was brief and ended in bitter sorrow, I would not have been without it—no, not for anything in the world. And I bless you because you have provided so well for our child. Farewell, then, and may you fare as well as is wished for you by your old faithful
Kristine. *

When Constance had read the letter, she lowered her face into her hands and sobbed. This poor woman with her child! Why had she been cast off? By what right did men behave in this way! They enjoyed these women’s youth, their health, their love, as though they had been created for this one purpose; they enjoyed them until they were sated. If they saw something more desirable, they flung them aside and abandoned them to the fate that the men’s brutal selfishness had prepared for them. She felt a profound compassion for this patiently suffering woman, who was so full of goodness and resignation, and at the same time a rebellious bitterness against the brutality of society that had made it so convenient and so safe for men to surrender themselves to their sexual lusts.

She no longer felt any jealousy; the nature of her pain was different; a violent aversion to her husband stirred within her, and she could not bear to think of him.

The other letters were from Lorck to Kristine; they were numbered, and she read them in order. She saw that it was a relationship that had lasted for several years, but that at the same time he had had love affairs on the side, as was evident from replies he had given to Kristine’s reproaches and outbursts of jealousy. One of these rivals had been a married lady and had evidently belonged to Lorck’s social circle. One of the letters said: “My beloved Kristine, just be easy; I shall come back to you after all. You must not trouble yourself about that silly affair. Had you not happened to learn of it, it could not have done you any harm. Besides, I am tired of this constant need to be on my guard against the husband, and after all she has never managed to take me entirely away from you. If she had not thrown herself at me with her love, I would never have come to think of her. I am happiest in your arms; you must remember that and believe it to be true. I really do love you, Kristine; you are so delicate and sweet and lovely—nota bene, when you are gentle and cheerful; it does not suit you to sulk and shed tears—do you hear, Kitten?”—

Amalie Skram: Constance Ring. 25

For the rest, the contents of most of the letters concerned arranging when she was to come to him, and so forth. They were full of words of love of the same kind as those he had given Constance, sometimes even precisely the very same expressions, and a cutting sensation passed through her.

Then there was a period of some months during which they had not corresponded, and then came a letter that began as follows: “Yes, my beloved, do come back to me, if you are as fresh and sweet as before; there is nothing I would rather have. When I advised you to become engaged to that fellow, it was because I thought it might lead to your happiness; now that you have sent him away, there is nothing separating us. You must believe that it was not with a light heart that I let you slip from my arms. What I have had to make do with in the meantime has not pleased me at all, and a lady in love with whom I became involved out of sheer boredom is leaving town one of these days.

“I am looking forward to having you back. Come tomorrow evening at ten, if you can. If I am not at home, just lie down and go quietly to sleep as in the old days, when I used to wake you with a kiss; you still have the little key, after all. And listen, I have had the bathroom put in order; it has become so inviting—you shall see what a capable bath attendant I shall be.” Then came a series of letters, more loving and tender than ever, with an undercurrent of sadness; she was his comfort and refuge, they said. Constance calculated that they dated from the time when he was courting her. And then came the point when Kristine had been pregnant. She read his expressions of regret, which appeared to have been dictated by genuine compassion, and were studded with phrases intended as grounds for consolation. At last came the final one. It contained a brief farewell; he was to travel abroad, and it was uncertain when he would return home, or whether he would ever do so at all. He asked her to collect the monthly allowance for the child from Lawyer Hansen, who knew all about it and had instructions to begin the payments whenever she requested it. Finally, he advised her to marry someone who, it appeared, had made her an offer of marriage, and declared that he was willing to give her money for her trousseau.

25*

When Constance had finished reading, she cut the broken sealing-wax seal from the wrapper and carefully wrapped up the letters; she found some string, which she wound around the packet, and locked it and the letter from Hansen in her drawer. Then she sat down with her elbows on the table and her face in her hands. For about ten minutes she remained motionless. Suddenly she seemed to collect herself and stood up; her cheeks were ashen, and her lips had become so strangely thin; her fingers clawed across the tablecloth as though with a vague notion that they had to seize hold of something. Had Lorck seen her at that moment, he would have had difficulty recognizing his wife in this rigid figure with the deep furrow between the staring eyes and the slack features. She stole quietly back to the bedroom, but despite her caution the door made a squeaking sound that woke Lorck.

Meanwhile, Ring paced about at home in the most agonizing anxiety. When Alette heard the mistress leave the house, she went back in to him and stood sobbing with her apron before her eyes. He had brought ruin upon her; now the mistress would dismiss her—why had he not let her remain what she had been? Before, she had conducted herself like a decent girl, and now! Oh, dear Jesus, that things should go this way for her—what was to become of her now? There was nothing for it but to go straight off and cast herself away— Ring promised not to abandon her and asked her merely to remain calm and do her work as though nothing had happened. He would see if he could smooth matters over so that nothing more came of it.

Then he walked up and down the sitting room, stopping every now and then and cursing the damned accident that had played him such an intricate trick. He writhed at the thought of all that he would have to go through with Constance. She would not be merciful, he thought, but in the end he consoled himself that it would all blow over after some time had passed. At this point in his reflections, he felt the need to revive himself with a glass of cognac and water. Why was Constance always like that—it was her fault that things went so badly. Why did they not live together like two turtledoves?

Every moment he was at the window peering out; now and then he stood out in the entrance hall and listened.

The longer it went on, the more uneasy he became; his mouth was drawn into a sullen grimace, his eyebrows formed a sharp angle, and his forehead lay in thick, baggy folds. He dreaded terribly the moment when she would enter and was at the same time in torment because she did not come.

At last he heard someone at the front door. He went out and opened it.

Constance passed him calmly and began taking off her outer garments. Then she went into the sitting room, sat down on the sofa, and picked up the evening paper.

Ring sank onto a chair some distance away and remained sitting bent forward, with his elbow on his knee and his hand shading his eyes. Now and then he glanced over at his wife, but lacked the courage to address her.

At last he gathered his courage and said, “Can you forgive me, Constance?”

She put the newspaper aside, looked at him as though about to say something, but gave it up and took up the paper again.

“This day shall be a turning point in my life,” he began.

“Spare me your phrases,” she said dryly. “I cannot bear to listen to them.”

“I know I have offended you cruelly,” he stammered, “and I will accept whatever penance you impose upon me—whatever—”

“What I have to say is not much,” she interrupted him with a motion of her hand. “When you are having relations with my servant girl—”

“I am not having relations with anyone.”

“When you are having relations with my servant girl, then it goes without saying that I wish to be spared your company. If you want her—then by all means, but then you must leave me in peace. I have consented to be your wife—that is bad enough, but I will not be one of your mistresses.” She rose and made to leave the room.

Ring thought she had never been so lovely and so desirable as at that moment. She was an entirely different woman. A terror of losing her shot through his mind like a vicious stab; he sprang up and placed himself in her way.

“Scorn me, trample on me, spit on me, kill me!” he cried. “I am a wretch, a miserable fellow who did not know what a treasure I possessed, a man unworthy to untie your shoelace, but I love you, Constance—no, let me speak—I love and adore you; I lie in the dust and kiss your feet—I care for no one in the world but you, whatever you may believe.” He held his hands to his head and writhed as though in convulsions.

“Nonsense,” she said with a grimace. “You bore me.”

“Yes, I know it—I know it, and that is my eternal torment. You have never loved me, not in the least. And then at times you have behaved in such a way that I almost had to imagine that you cared for me—I have been in a maze, I have. Oh, Constance, if you had loved me, you could have made a different man of me. How I have languished for your love; that is what is to blame.” His voice was lost in weeping. He sank to his knees and hid his face in her dress.

“Get up—you are drunk,” she said unwillingly.

“I am just as sober at this moment as you yourself, Constance.” He looked up at her with the look of a punished dog. “I will not get up; I shall lie here until you say that you have forgiven me.”

Constance felt a fellow human being’s compassion for him; it pained her to see him so humiliated. “But how do you expect me to be able to believe you?” she said.

“No, Constance—it is true, it is all too true—oh, but do it nevertheless, this one time, and you shall have thanks and honor for it; when you have once come to trust me anew, and perhaps feel a kind of affection for me because for many years I have been undemanding and faithful and have never complained, then it will do you good to think that it was you who saved me. Do not thrust me away, for without you I shall perish.” He was still on his knees, holding her dress in both hands and kissing it.

Constance was caught up in this deep emotion. She bowed her head and began to weep.

“There is an old saying that it is better to give than to receive,” he continued in the same passionately pleading voice. “Look at me, Constance, lying here and begging, while you stand there so far above me and hold my fate in your hand; do not be merciless, but let yourself be moved, Constance.”

“It is not out of hardness,” she said in a tearful voice, “but what has happened cannot simply be erased from our lives.”

“Yes, it can, it can, Constance; oh, try, try—receive me back into your favor and put me on trial.”

“Get up and sit down—I want to ask you something.”

He obeyed like a schoolboy. She took a seat directly opposite him.

“Then let me know how far things have gone between you and her.”

“Gone? They have not gone anywhere at all. What could they have gone to, apart from what you saw? That is bad enough.”

The sound of the hall bell broke in upon the silence and brought her back to the present with a violent jolt. The maid came and said that there was a gentleman asking whether he might be permitted to see Madam. Constance took the card she held out to her.

“Let him come in,” she said breathlessly, fumbling for something in her pocket. During the one minute that passed before Mejer appeared on the threshold, Constance had risen and sat down again several times.

She held out her hand to him.

“It was delightful to see You,” she said nervously. “How are You?”

Mejer stood working at something in his throat that obstructed his words, while he pressed her warm hand with his cold fingers.

“I met Your husband a short while ago; he asked me to come up and see how You were living.”

“Had You not thought of doing so Yourself, then?”

“I did not know—I thought... Are You already settled?”

Constance regained her composure; the pallor had left her face; a delicate red color had come into her cheeks, and her eyes shone with their loveliest brilliance.

“Completely,” she answered. “This is my room. Would You like to see the others?”

He went ahead. “Here is Lorck’s department,” she said when they had passed through the dining room. “Here You shall see: waiting room, reception room, and study.” The last was a small room with a window facing the side street, packed full of books and handsome upholstered oak furniture.

“And here is Your territory?” Mejer asked when they had finished the inspection.

“Yes, this is my room. Is it not cozy?”

“Incredibly so! And with You as its resident.—I do not know whether it is because the room is Yours, or because You are the room’s, that it looks so enchanting.”

She bent down and brushed a speck of dust from her dress.

“Let us try what it is like to sit in it,” she said, pushing a chair toward him.

“Imagine that it is only three days since we arrived,” Mejer began as he sat down.

“Yes, can You comprehend it?” Constance interrupted. “It seems like months to me.”

“Eternities!” He flung out his hand. “Yesterday and today have refused to come to an end; it is because I have not seen You, Constance.”

She shifted slightly in her chair. “It has seemed so long to me as well,” she said.

“I have been walking about fantasizing about coming up here,” he began again, “and then I have longed for You so intensely that in the end I grew accustomed to it and thought it was so good to have something to long for.”

“You speak as though You had been going on like this for years,” she said with a smile.

“And I have incessantly had to think of You as You were on the deck at night—incessantly,” he repeated with emphasis.

“But You must forget that, Mejer.” There was something pleading in her voice. “We are to be friends, only friends; promise me that You will treat me as such.” She raised her eyes and fixed them on him.

Mejer did not answer at once; he sat losing himself in how lovely she was; it was so sweet to hear her voice, to be so near her, and to feel her eyes upon his face.

“You do promise me, do You not?” she added.

“Oh no, spare me! I cannot decide in advance to be this way or that toward You.” His tone was plaintive.

She began to consider his words and stared before her, shaking her head anxiously.

“I have loved You all my life, from the first time I saw You, and I have suffered to a degree of which You have no conception. Give me leave to be as I can and must.” He had risen and was now standing before her. “I will do You no harm”—a melancholy note entered his voice. “You do believe that, do You not?”

She lowered her eyes; her fingers picked at the lace on her overdress.

“You do believe that, do You not?” he repeated more earnestly.

She looked up at him and smiled sorrowfully.

“Yes,” she said, slowly shaking her head. “But Mejer, Mejer, how will this end!” She rose and hurried across the floor.

“End! Why are You thinking of that? Come what may!” he cried passionately. “I am Yours—You possess me; do You hear, Constance? You possess me!”

She held her hands over her ears and shook her head while looking at him with frightened eyes.

“You must not be afraid, Constance”—he spoke more calmly and moved closer to her. “Do I look like a robber or a burglar? I would sooner cut off my right hand than stretch it out to seize You when You had not freely given me permission.”

She began pacing the floor, and Mejer could see that a struggle was taking place within her.

“You shall learn to feel safe with me, Constance—no one in the world can be more tender toward You than I.” He held out his hands to her.

She stopped before him, took both his hands, and pressed them tightly for a moment.

“You must be good, Mejer, only good,” she said in a low voice, looking fearfully into his eyes.

481

Then she released his hands and began once more to walk up and down.

“Constance, I have one request of You: call me Harald when we are alone,” he pleaded. “Oh, do it, Constance.”

She nodded and continued walking.

“Someone is coming.” She went over and opened the door.

“Has Mejer not been here?” Lorck’s voice asked from the entrance hall.

“He is sitting in here,” was the answer. Over her shoulder she sent him a glance that said: Do sit down. He felt electrically touched; after all, it was an acknowledgment of their secret understanding.

“Well, what do you say, Mejer? Is it not quite habitable here?”

Lorck had stepped inside and looked around with satisfaction.

They spoke for a while about the rooms’ excellent location, about the advantage of having the morning sun, and about other such things.

“So we shall move home this evening, then, Constance,” Lorck said when Mejer had left. “You will come down to the hotel with me and pack our things, I suppose?”

“Yes, then let us set off at once,” she answered.

“Oh no, wait a little; it is so cozy here.” He began opening the doors. “It looks positively elegant when all the rooms stand open.” He rubbed his hands contentedly and sat down where he could survey the whole.

482

“And how capable you have been! Come over to me, Constance. Is it not delightful to be at home in our own pretty home?”

“Yes,” she said absently.

He pressed her down onto his knee, took hold of her hands, and began gently rocking her up and down while humming: “Ride, ride, ranke.”

“No, no—stop—I must go out and speak to the maid.” She quickly freed herself.

“Did he say anything to you about it, then?” Constance asked with a half-roguish, half-wondering smile.

“No indeed, not one blessed whit,” Lorck assured her. “It may well be that it was merely a fancy of mine; I went around thinking that everyone must fall in love with you, you see.”

They both remained silent for a few minutes.

“What are you thinking about, my Conny?” Lorck then said, reaching for her hand.

“Nothing, really,” she said kindly.

“Nonsense, tell me now,” he begged, drawing her closer to him.

“Well, that is easier said than done. Sometimes one’s thoughts run so wild, or they come in little fragments and are so disconnected, or it is sheer foolishness that one sits there being driven around by; it is quite impossible to find words for it.”

He had put his arm around her waist and, with his other hand, bent her head in toward him so that it came to rest against his neck. They held each other in an embrace and sat for a while without speaking.

“But now I know what I am thinking about,” said Constance, pressing her lips against his beard.

“What, then, Conny?”

“About what we have spoken of so often: about how happy you have made me, about all our treasures, about everything we have lived through together, about the love you have brought to life in me by loving me, and especially about what you know—the thing that lies ahead.”

“My beloved, sweet one,” Lorck said, pressing her closer to him. “How happy you make me; how blissful your words are, and how sweet your caresses. And you, who were so afraid to take me—” he added a little later in a more tender voice.

“Not you any more than others; I felt reluctance or aversion, in general.”

“And in the beginning, when we were married—do you remember how foolish I was, utterly miserable with shyness?”

“Really, I have been rather persevering, Conny; you must admit that, for you did everything to discourage me. But, as I said, I loved you. I had never loved before I began to love you.”

“Is that really true, Nils? Tell me, is it true?”

“Yes, my dear, I know that now. If it had not been for you, I would never have learned to know love. And now, when we are expecting our treasure, I am supremely happy, Conny.”

“But you have nevertheless been in love with others—yes, and had relations with others?”

“It was nonsense and folly, Conny. Only you have made life come alive for me.”

“And it is the same for you too, Conny,” he continued a little later. “Your life begins only with me, does it not?”

She did not answer.

“For you love me; say that you love me.”

“You know I do, Nils,” she said softly.

“But say it all the same; it is so sweet to hear.”

A strange sensation came over her. She felt an urge to shake his arms off her and run away. It was as though something ghostly in the darkness were creeping up behind her, something she did not dare turn around to look at. It made her shudder. And then, at that same moment, she remembered the gentle pleasure that had stolen over her when Mejer, quite by chance that day, happened to place his arm on the back of the chair in which she was sitting. But now she wanted to get away from all this, and with a leap she plunged into the realm of thoughts of love and happiness in which she had lived for all these many months. She wrapped the memories of the sweet hours and all the enchanting little things that had passed between her and Lorck around herself like a shield. She would be happy, and that was that.

“I love you,” she said, “love, love you,” and her kisses and caresses were more passionate than ever before.

Lorck pressed her to his heart with a rapturous smile on his half-open lips. She hid her face in his soft, thick beard.

“But what is this?” he said with a sudden start. “I am becoming ill.” He grasped her hand and bent forward, groaning. Violent chills ran through him.

“You have caught cold from that ice,” said Constance. “Come, let us go up.”

With difficulty he rose and, supported by Constance’s arm, walked up through the garden and into the hotel; from time to time he stood still and moaned with pain.

When they had reached their rooms, Constance was alarmed by his pallor; a cold sweat lay on his brow, and he complained of unbearable nausea. She immediately sent for a doctor.

He was a somewhat elderly, short, stocky little Frenchman with masses of gray hair and beard. He told Constance that her husband had caught a severe cold, but that he hoped it would not become serious. Then he promised to send some medicine and to return the next morning.

XXV.

Lorck lay ill with gastric fever. Constance nursed him with tireless care. Most of the time he did not recognize her, but took her for someone else; he frequently called her Kristine.

The doctor obtained a deaconess who was to keep watch every other night, taking turns with Constance. He believed that three or four weeks would pass before they could even think about the journey home; otherwise there was no danger, provided only that they observed caution.

He gave a start. “You! I do not understand what you mean by that,” he stammered, groping for words. “Oh, you are only joking,” he then said, with a sudden movement toward her.

“No, I am not joking. What I am saying is true, and now I shall see whether you are willing to believe me when I assure you that it does not matter in the least, and that you must be so good as to marry me all the same.”

“So you do want me, then?” he cried jubilantly and sprang up. But then he sank back onto the bench and remained sitting as if petrified.

“I suppose it is my turn now to ask whether you will?”

He did not answer, but merely sat staring down at his knees, where his hands lay. In the moonlight, which now poured all the way in to them, they looked even whiter than by day.

“A past,” he said at last, without moving.

“What kind of past?”

“I had some lovers when I was in Paris.”

“Some,” he twisted from side to side. “That was not exactly too few, either.”

“Yes, now you know. You see that I am just as candid as you are.”

“Yes, thank you, I will not claim that it exactly pleases me.” He spoke so softly that Henny could barely hear what he said. “Lovers?—Whom you lived with like that?”

“Yes, whom I lived with.”

“Frenchmen?”

“Yes, no. Well, one of them was French.”

“And the others?”

“Oh, surely it can be all the same to you.”

“All the same!” He sprang up, flailing his arms. “Strangle them, murder them, kick them to death!” he ground out through his teeth. “Hack them to pieces, throw their limbs into the sea. Blood! Blood!—Oh, to think that those scoundrels have taken thy pure innocence, Henny”—his voice changed; it trembled and seemed to dissolve into lamentation. He slid back down onto the bench and resumed his former posture.

His violent outburst had frightened Henny. She had risen and held out her arm as if to hush him. Now she sat down again and said, “In that way the match is more equal, I should think. Equals play best together.”

Knut remained completely motionless for a while. Henny looked at him from the side. Suddenly she noticed his head sinking onto his chest, and immediately afterward she heard him weeping quietly.

She rose and stood in front of him.

“You have not answered my question as to whether you will still have me in spite of it,” she said, laying her hand on his shoulder.

“Whether I will have thee, Henny?” He looked up at her; his eyes were full of tears, and there were wet streaks on his cheeks. “To ask such a thing—oh, but it hurts so much, so much.” His voice choked, and he had to wait a little before he regained control of it. “If thou wert living here in town as the vilest fallen woman, Henny, I would still beg thee on my knees to take me as thy husband.” His head was bent back, and the moonlight fell across his pale face as he looked up into Henny’s eyes with a helpless gaze. “I know well that thou hast never believed in my love—dost thou believe in it now?”

Henny was violently agitated. Her breast rose and fell, and she gasped for breath as she struggled to get the words out. But she could not. Then she gave up, stretched out her arms, clasped Knut around the neck, and sank against his breast with her face hidden at his neck.

“Yes, Knut, now I believe in thy love. And I love thee too. I believe in thee, and I am thine. Since thou wilt have me.”

“Thank thee, my beloved,” he whispered.

“And now I shall tell thee something, Knut”—Henny had mastered her emotion and now sat on the bench beside Knut with her hand in his. “It is all pure invention.”

“What is invention?”

“The business about the lovers, of course, thou fool. It shows at once how young thou art. I only wanted to put thee to the test. Thou hast passed it like a man. I am proud of thee, Knut.”

“Is it true, Henny?” he said hoarsely, pressing her hand against his heart.

“Of course it is true—unfortunately, I almost said. Karen claims, you know, that only those marriages are happy in which the woman too has a past.”

Very quietly Knut slipped from the bench onto his knees, hid his face in Henny’s lap, and sobbed like a child.

Henny caressingly ran her fingers through his thick, soft hair and soothed him. “My own boy, my sweet, good Knut, my dear, only beloved—now thou must be happy, thou must.”

“It was the joy,” Knut said in a faint voice and rose. “Thou shouldst not have done it, Henny. Just think if I had suffered a stroke.” He quickly rubbed his face with his handkerchief.

“But where dost thou think Karen imagines I have got to?” Henny then said. “Come, let us go down and fetch the lamp.” She sprang down the veranda steps, followed by Knut.

When Henny had entered the summerhouse, she sat down on the bench and gleefully rubbed her palms together. “So now I am an engaged girl—oh, how delightful! It was not too soon, either. But thou—oh, how Karen’s eyes will pop.”

“Yes,” Knut said. “She probably did not believe thou wouldst have me.”

“As was only reasonable! But what dost thou look like, Knut! Red blotches on thy cheeks—and what has become of thine eyes? I say”—she rushed over to him and shook him by the shoulders—“why hast thou not kissed me? On the mouth, I mean.” She pursed her lips and held them up toward him.

He drew his head slightly back and took hold of her wrists. “I will not do it tonight, Henny, for I kissed another woman earlier today.”

“No, really, Knut! Thou art too disgusting!” Henny knitted her brows and freed her wrists. “Whom didst thou kiss?”

“That Mrs. Gerner.”

“The Tivoli lady! Here at our house! Tonight? Then thou art having an affair with her.”

“Not in the least. I have only been with her once before and have not thought of her for a moment in the meantime.”

“Then it is a thousand times worse. So that is the sort thou art! Art thou not ashamed?”

“Oh yes. A little.”

“Kissed the Tivoli lady! When? How couldst thou get the chance to do it, thou disgusting creature?”

“When we walked in the park.”

“So thou took advantage at once. Yes, that is like thee. And that just when thou wert about to propose to me?”

“Thou received me so scornfully. ‘Naturally nothing will come of it tonight either,’ I thought, and so I did it out of spite.”

“But what about her—is she still the sort who lets herself be kissed?”

“Yes, who does not? And she, especially!”

“The hussy! Karen ought to know that. And thou—yes, what a splendid husband I shall be getting.” Henny put her arms behind her back and leaned with one shoulder at an angle against the wall of the summerhouse close to the entrance. She looked threateningly at Knut.

He had come all the way up into Vestre Aker before he turned around and walked downhill again. He wanted to go up to Lucie and make peace with her—oh, how he burned for her now. He took long strides and went almost at a run down the hills. It was a good thing no one saw him.

This was how he always felt when he was away from her. Every drop of blood in him cried out for her, especially when there had been a tangle in the thread between them. He might just as well have spared himself the trouble of walking away that evening. He ought to have known that he would end up running like a madman to shorten the minutes of their separation. His head was burning, so that a couple of times he took off his hat to cool himself, and he sighed as an oppressed man sighs. For even now, when he was glowing with love and desire, he felt at the same time that dull rancor which always lay digging away inside him, that searing bitterness toward his love, that painful, jealous hatred of those who had had her before him, and finally the resentment that he, lawyer Theodor Gerner, was held captive in a relationship that caused him anguish and that he knew he did not have the strength to break off. He had gone up there that evening determined to tell her that she was to become his wife, but no sooner did he see her than he grew uncertain and thought it could wait until another time. It was also only when he was away from her that marrying seemed unavoidable to him. When he was with her, he thought things were good as they were.

Yes, but for that very reason, he stopped and placed his forefinger against his nose. With her you are content; away from her you are a man without peace. What is there to hesitate over, then?

A few minutes later he was at the street door of her building, for which he always carried the key in his pocket. Ugh, that disgusting entrance, with the middle gate always open onto the filthy courtyard, where the long row of numbered privy doors stood directly opposite, on display. And those loathsome stairs, which smelled of gutters and kerosene, with their spattered, churchlike windows and their gray walls, which had holes in the whitewash, with cobwebs and dust hanging down like mourning crape. How tired he was of it all! Those doors on every floor, one on either side and one directly opposite, with cracked porcelain plates and black calling cards and patterned panes of frosted glass, and the green bell cords with frayed passementerie handles and mats full of holes in front of the doors.

Quickly and quietly he let himself into the entrance hall, hung up his hat, and opened the door to the sitting room. God knows why she has the lamp burning when it is so light, he thought, looking around for Lucie. Oh, how good it would be never again to have to enter these ugly, oblong rooms with their pink walls and ornate ceilings, and these vile, tiered stoves.

Lucie was lying on the sofa with her arms folded across her breast, staring straight ahead with wide-open eyes, without giving any sign whatever that she heard him come in.

“Well, Lucie,” he said tenderly, drawing a chair over to the sofa with his foot and sitting down on it. “I can well understand that it must sometimes be lonely for you, but if you have nothing else, there is always me to wait for.” He bent over her and kissed her.

She put one arm around his neck and pleaded with her lips for his mouth, until she felt his kiss against her teeth.

“Oh God, how I love you, Theodor,” she whispered. “Yes, you don’t know it, even though you are so nasty and cruel to me.” She pinched his earlobe. “Why do you have to be like that, you horrid thing?”

“You take too little care of yourself, my dear. You must know that it is you who always provokes me. But you are still the dearest thing in the world to me. Come now, I want to go to bed, and then I shall confide something to you.” He straightened up with a hurried movement and pushed the table aside to make room for her. At that moment his eyes fell on Nilsen’s letter, which Lucie had left at the top of the sewing basket.

“What is this?” He picked up the letter and read: Dear, precious miss and maiden!

“A love letter, as you can see.” Lucie had begun to unbutton her dress and went into the bedroom without closing the door behind her. “Are we going to start in about Nilsen again?” she thought.

When Theodor had read the letter, he let it fall onto the table, took out his fine, red-edged handkerchief, and carefully rubbed his fingers on it. He remained standing for a while, lost in thought, looking out through half-closed eyes with a dark and troubled gaze.

“Aren’t you coming now, Theodor?” From the creaking of the feather mattress, he could hear Lucie jumping into bed. “That wretched letter! It’s nothing to stand there lost in thought over, after all.”

Gerner ran a hand over his face and went into the bedroom.

“Why haven’t you told me that you have a suitor?” he asked, sitting down on the chair in front of the bed.

“No, you are much too comical, Theodor! Surely you don’t mean—” She burst out laughing.

“It is most regrettable that you do not have that much confidence in me,” Gerner continued. “I had deserved that much from you. Letting them come here and court you. What kind of scoundrel is he?”

Lucie had stopped laughing. Her heart was beating hard, and her voice sounded a little hoarse when she answered: “He runs errands for the Tivoli performers in the afternoons, and in the mornings he is a messenger at a bank or something like that.”

“Have you had anything to do with him in the past?” It sounded as though it pained him to force the words out.

“He has never even laid a finger on me. You always have to think that, too.”

“When did he begin making his declarations?”

“It was a long time ago now,” Lucie answered in an embarrassed tone.

“And you have let him go on! You only had to say one word to me. I would have taught him to keep his nose away from you. Why have you kept quiet about it?”

“I wanted nothing whatever to do with him then. Surely you understand that. In letters.”

“Then? What do you mean by that?”

“One has to think about the future too,” she said plaintively. “What is to become of me in this world?”

“Could you really bring yourself to marry that man?”

“That would be the most sensible thing, after all.”

Gerner sat perfectly still, his face turned toward Lucie, looking at her in the twilight of the summer night. She lay on her back with her throat and arms bare, picking at the top sheet.

“It does not happen very often to the likes of me that an honest man wants to marry one,” Lucie continued, with short pauses between her words. “And is it so strange if I think: You had better try to resign yourself to it, for there will probably be nothing else for you in this world, and in time you will surely forget Theodor, if you work very hard at it.”

'Next week we'll go to a photographer's in London and have my little
girl done,' said Wemyss, pushing open the library door, 'and then I'll
have her exactly as God made her, without some artist idiot or other
coming butting-in with his idea of her. God's idea of her is good enough
for me. They won't have to enlarge much,' he laughed, 'to get _you_
life-size, you midge. Vera was five foot ten. Now isn't this a fine
room? Look--there's the river. Isn't it jolly being so close to it? Come
round here--don't knock against my writing-table, now. Look--there's
only the towpath between the river and the garden. Lord, what a beastly
day. It might just as easily have been a beautiful spring day and us
having our coffee out on the terrace. Don't you think this is a
beautiful look-out,--so typically English with the beautiful green lawn
and the bit of lush grass along the towpath, and the river. There's no
river like it in the world, is there, little Love. Say you think it's
the most beautiful river in the world'--he hugged her close--'say you
think it's a hundred times better than that beastly French one we got so
sick of with all those châteaux.'

'Oh, a _hundred_ times better,' said Lucy.

They were standing at the window, with his arm round her shoulder. There
was just room for them between it and the writing-table. Outside was the
flagged terrace, and then a very green lawn with worms and blackbirds on
it and a flagged path down the middle leading to a little iron gate.
There was no willow hedge along the river end of the square garden, so
as not to interrupt the view,--only the iron railings and wire-netting.
Terra-cotta vases, which later on would be a blaze of geraniums, Wemyss
explained, stood at intervals on each side of the path. The river,
swollen and brown, slid past Wemyss's frontage very quickly that day,
for there had been much rain. The clouds scudding across the sky before
the wind were not in such a hurry but that every now and then they let
loose a violent gust of rain, soaking the flags of the terrace again just
as the wind had begun to dry them up. How could he stand there, she
thought, holding her tight so that she couldn't get away, making her
look out at the very place on those flags not two yards off....

But the next minute she thought how right he really was, how absolutely
the only way this was to do the thing. Perfect simplicity was the one
way to meet this situation successfully; and she herself was so far from
simplicity that here she was shrinking, not able to bear to look,
wanting only to hide her face,--oh, he was wonderful, and she was the
most ridiculous of fools.

She pressed very close to him, and put up her face to his, shutting her
eyes, for so she shut out the desolating garden with its foreground of
murderous flags.

'What is it, little Love?' asked Wemyss.

'Kiss me,' she said; and he laughed and kissed her, but hastily, because
he wanted her to go on admiring the view.

She still, however, held up her face. 'Kiss my eyes,' she whispered,
keeping them shut. 'They're tired----'

He laughed again, but with a slight impatience, and kissed her eyes; and
then, suddenly struck by her little blind face so close to his, the
strong light from the big window showing all its delicate curves and
delicious softnesses, his Lucy's face, his own little wife's, he kissed
her really, as she loved him to kiss her, becoming absorbed only in his
love.

'Oh, I love you, love you----' murmured Lucy, clinging to him, making
secret vows of sensibleness, of wholesomeness, of a determined,
unfailing future simplicity.

'Aren't we happy,' he said, pausing in his kisses to gaze down at what
was now his face, for was it not much more his than hers? Of course it
was his. She never saw it, except when she specially went to look, but
he saw it all the time; she only had duties in regard to it, but he was
on the higher plane of only having joys. She washed it, but he kissed
it. And he kissed it when he liked and as much as ever he liked. 'Isn't
it wonderful being married,' he said, gazing down at this delightful
thing that was his very own for ever.

'Oh--wonderful!' murmured Lucy, opening her eyes and gazing into his.

Her face broke into a charming smile. 'You have the dearest eyes,' she
said, putting up her finger and gently tracing his eyebrows with it.

Wemyss's eyes, full at that moment of love and pride, were certainly
dear eyes, but a noise at the other end of the room made Lucy jump so in
his arms, gave her apparently such a fright, that when he turned his
head to see who it was daring to interrupt them, daring to startle his
little girl like that, and beheld the parlourmaid, his eyes weren't dear
at all but very angry.

The parlourmaid had come in with the coffee; and seeing the two
interlaced figures against the light of the big window had pulled up
short, uncertain what to do. This pulling up had jerked a spoon off its
saucer onto the floor with a loud rattle because of the floor not having
a carpet on it and being of polished oak, and it was this noise that
made Lucy jump so excessively that her jump actually made Wemyss jump
too.

In the parlourmaid's untrained phraseology there had been a good deal of
billing and cooing during luncheon, and even in the hall before luncheon
there were examples of it, but what she found going on in the library
was enough to make anybody stop dead and upset things,--it was such, she
said afterwards in the kitchen, that if she didn't know for a fact that
they were really married she wouldn't have believed it. Married people
in the parlourmaid's experience didn't behave like that. What affection
there was was exhibited before, and not after, marriage. And she went on
to describe the way in which Wemyss--thus briefly and irreverently did
they talk of their master in the kitchen--had flown at her for having
come into the library. 'After telling me to,' she said. 'After saying,
"We'll 'ave coffee in the library."' And they all agreed, as they had
often before agreed, that if it weren't that he was in London half the
time they wouldn't stay in the place five minutes.

Meanwhile Wemyss and Lucy were sitting side by side in two enormous
chairs facing the unlit library fire drinking their coffee. The fire was
only lit in the evenings, explained Wemyss, after the 1st of April; the
weather ought to be warm enough by then to do without fires in the
daytime, and if it wasn't it was its own look-out.

The dining-room was a narrow room full of a table. It had a window
facing west and a window facing north, and in spite of the uninterrupted
expanses of plate glass was a bleak, dark room. But then the weather was
bleak and dark, and one saw such a lot of it out of the two big windows
as one sat at the long table and watched the rolling clouds blowing
straight towards one from the north-west; for Lucy's place was facing
the north window, on Wemyss's left hand. Wemyss sat at the end of the
table facing the west window. The table was so long that if Lucy had
sat in the usual seat of wives, opposite her husband, communication
would have been difficult,--indeed, as she remarked, she would have
disappeared below the dip of the horizon.

'I like a long table,' said Wemyss to this. 'It looks so hospitable.'

'Yes,' said Lucy a little doubtfully, but willing to admit that its
length at least showed a readiness for hospitality. 'I suppose it does.
Or it would if there were people all round it.'

'People? You don't mean to say you want people already?'

'Good heavens no,' said Lucy hastily. 'Of course I don't. Why, of
course, Everard, I didn't mean that,' she added, laying her hand on his
and smiling at him so as to dispel the gathering cloud on his face; and
once more she flung all thoughts of the parlourmaid to the winds. 'You
know I don't want a soul in the world but you.'

'Well, that's what I thought,' said Wemyss, mollified. 'I know all I
want is you.'

(Was this same parlourmaid here in Vera's time? Lucy asked herself very
privately and unconsciously and beneath the concerned attentiveness she
was concentrating on Wemyss.)

'What lovely kingcups!' she said aloud.

'Oh yes, there they are--I hadn't noticed them. Yes, aren't they?
They're my birthday flowers.' And he repeated his formula: 'It's my
birthday and Spring's.'

But Lucy, of course, didn't know the proper ritual, it being her first
experience of one of Wemyss's birthdays, besides having wished him his
many happy returns hours ago when he first opened his eyes and found
hers gazing at him with love; so all she did was to make the natural but
unfortunate remark that surely Spring began on the 21st of March,--or
was it the 25th? No, that was Christmas Day--no, she didn't mean
that----

'You're always saying things and then saying you didn't mean them,'
interrupted Wemyss, vexed, for he thought that Lucy of all people should
have recognised the allegorical nature of his formula. If it had been
Vera, now,--but even Vera had managed to understand that much. 'I wish
you would begin with what you do mean, it would be so much simpler.
What, pray, _do_ you mean now?'

'I can't think,' said Lucy timidly, for she had offended him again, and
this time she couldn't even remotely imagine how.




XVII


He got over it, however. There was a particularly well-made soufflé, and
this helped. Also Lucy kept on looking at him very tenderly, and it was
the first time she had sat at his table in his beloved home, realising
the dreams of months that she should sit just there with him, his little
bobbed-haired Love, and gradually therefore he recovered and smiled at
her again.

But what power she had to hurt him, thought Wemyss; it was so great
because his love for her was so great. She should be very careful how
she wielded it. Her Everard was made very sensitive by his love.

He gazed at her solemnly, thinking this, while the plates were being
changed.

'What is it, Everard?' Lucy asked anxiously.

'I'm only thinking that I love you,' he said, laying his hand on hers.

She flushed with pleasure, and her face grew instantly happy. 'My
Everard,' she murmured, gazing back at him, forgetful in her pleasure of
the parlourmaid. How dear he was. How silly she was to be so much
distressed when he was offended. At the core he was so sound and simple.
At the core he was utterly her own dear lover. The rest was mere
incident, merest indifferent detail.

'We'll have coffee in the library,' he said to the parlourmaid, getting
up when he had finished his lunch and walking to the door. 'Come along,
little Love,' he called over his shoulder.

The library....

'Can't we--don't we--have coffee in the hall?' asked Lucy, getting up
slowly.

'No,' said Wemyss, who had paused before an enlarged photograph that
hung on the wall between the two windows, enlarged to life size.

He examined it a moment, and then drew his finger obliquely across the
glass from top to bottom. It then became evident that the picture needed
dusting.

'Look,' he said to the parlourmaid, pointing.

The parlourmaid looked.

'I notice you don't say anything,' he said to her after a silence in
which she continued to look, and Lucy, taken aback again, stood
uncertain by the chair she had got up from. 'I don't wonder. There's
nothing you can possibly say to excuse such carelessness.'

'Lizzie----' began the parlourmaid.

'Don't put it on to Lizzie.'

The parlourmaid ceased putting it on to Lizzie and was dumb.

'Come along, little Love,' said Wemyss, turning to Lucy and holding out
his hand. 'It makes one pretty sick, doesn't it, to see that not even
one's own father gets dusted.'

'Is that your father?' asked Lucy, hurrying to his side and offering no
opinion about dusting.

It could have been no one else's. It was Wemyss grown very enormous,
Wemyss grown very old, Wemyss displeased. The photograph had been so
arranged that wherever you moved to in the room Wemyss's father watched
you doing it. He had been watching Lucy from between those two windows
all through her first lunch, and must, flashed through Lucy's brain,
have watched Vera like that all through her last one.

'How long has he been there?' she asked, looking up into Wemyss's
father's displeased eyes which looked straight back into hers.

'Been there?' repeated Wemyss, drawing her away for he wanted his
coffee. 'How can I remember? Ever since I've lived here, I should think.
He died five years ago. He was a wonderful old man, nearly ninety. He
used to stay here a lot.'

Opposite this picture hung another, next to the door that led into the
hall,--also a photograph enlarged to life-size. Lucy had noticed neither
of these pictures when she came in, because the light from the windows
was in her eyes. Now, turning to go out through the door led by Wemyss,
she was faced by this one.

It was Vera. She knew at once; and if she hadn't she would have known
the next minute, because he told her.

'Vera,' he said, in a matter-of-fact tone, as it were introducing them.

'Vera,' repeated Lucy under her breath; and she and Vera--for this
photograph too followed one about with its eye--stared at each other.
